A code cell makes a figure when it has a `fig-` label and a `fig-cap`. The
class goes in `#| classes:`, and the width in `#| out-width:`. This page
shows the cell with its options:

## Result

The data are the `cars` data set that ships with R: the speed of each car
and the distance that it took to stop. This paragraph comes before the
cell, so it runs the full width of the text.


::: {.cell .wrap-right}

````{.cell-code}
```{{r}}
#| label: fig-cars
#| fig-cap: "Stopping distance by speed."
#| classes: wrap-right
#| out-width: "40%"
plot(cars, pch = 19, col = "#3b6ea8",
     xlab = "Speed (mph)", ylab = "Stopping distance (ft)")
```
````

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Stopping distance by speed.](code-cell_files/figure-typst/fig-cars-1.png){#fig-cars width=40%}
:::
:::


@fig-cars comes from the R code above. The cell's code stays above the
figure, and the figure floats to the right of the paragraphs after the
cell.

Faster cars took longer to stop. The figure has the same caption, number,
and `@fig-` link as a figure written in markdown. The plot's size in R
sets its shape, and `out-width` scales it to 40% of the text width. The
site renders this page from results that Quarto
saved when the cell last ran, so the site does not need R to build it.
After the text passes the bottom of the figure, each line starts at the
left edge of the text again and runs under the figure, as the end of this
paragraph shows. Two columns or a table could not give this layout,
because the text in them stays in its own column from top to bottom.
